global_caveat: Guidance only. It does not replace first-aid training or the advice of the 000 operator. Call 000 first and follow the operator.

coverage_caveat.text: If there is no mobile coverage on any network, you cannot reach Triple Zero from a mobile phone. Your call can use any available mobile network, but not if none has coverage. Calls to 000 can also be made from a satellite phone. If you carry a registered PLB or EPIRB, use it. You cannot contact Triple Zero by SMS.

Western Australia Police Force - Outback travel

numbers.label: Triple Zero
numbers.when: Life-threatening or time-critical emergencies: someone is seriously injured or needs urgent medical help, your life or property is in danger, or you have just seen a serious accident or crime. Say police, fire or ambulance.
numbers.detail: Free from any phone. Works from fixed and mobile phones, satellite phones and certain VoIP services. On a mobile you do not need to unlock the keypad or enter a PIN. A Telstra operator answers and puts you through. A mobile must be in range of a mobile network, and the call can use any available network. Phones need 4G or 5G with VoLTE emergency calling because 3G is switched off. Do not test your phone by calling 000.

extra_sources.source_name: ACMA - Emergency calls
Department of Infrastructure - Emergency calls and the 3G switch-off (VoLTE)

numbers.label: Mobile phones only
numbers.when: From a mobile phone only. Reaches the same Triple Zero service as 000.
numbers.detail: Cannot be called from a landline or satellite phone. It does not work without mobile coverage, just like 000.

extra_sources.source_name: ACMA - Emergency calls

numbers.label: Text relay (TTY)
numbers.when: For people who are deaf or have a hearing or speech difficulty. Needs a TTY (textphone).
numbers.detail: National Relay Service. The NRS can also transfer a captioned, internet, SMS, video or voice relay call to Triple Zero. You cannot use SMS to reach 106 or 000.

extra_sources.source_name: ACMA - Emergency calls

numbers.label: SES, not life-threatening
numbers.when: Flood, storm and tsunami help that is not life-threatening. Life-threatening: call 000.
numbers.detail: State Emergency Service. You cannot reach the SES through 000, because 000 only transfers to police, fire or ambulance.

extra_sources.source_name: Triple Zero (Australian Government)

numbers.label: Police Assistance Line, not urgent
numbers.when: Non-urgent police matters, such as reporting a crime that has already happened. Not for emergencies.
numbers.detail: Does not replace 000. If a crime is happening now, or someone is hurt or in danger, call 000.

extra_sources.source_name: Victoria Police - Police Assistance Line

numbers.label: healthdirect, nurse advice
numbers.when: Non-urgent health advice from a registered nurse, 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.
numbers.detail: Known as NURSE-ON-CALL in Victoria. If someone is seriously injured or very unwell, call 000 and ask for an ambulance.

operator_script.title: What to tell the 000 operator
operator_script.intro: Stay calm, speak slowly and clearly, and stay on the line.
steps: A Telstra operator answers first. Say which service you need: police, fire or ambulance. If you need an interpreter, say your language.

Say exactly where to send help. Read out the coordinates from the My location panel, then the nearest town, state, road name or landmark. In remote areas, give nearby roads, landmarks and the property name. If you are driving, say which way you are heading and the last town you passed. The operator will ask for the town and state you are calling from.
Say what has happened.
Say how many people are hurt, and whether they are awake and breathing.
Follow the operator's instructions and do not hang up until told to.
If it is not safe to speak, or you cannot speak, stay on the line. When the recorded message asks you to press 55, do that and you will be put through to police.

location_note.text: GPS can work with no phone signal, but it can take a minute or more to settle, so wait in the open if you can. This panel only shows where you are. It does not send your location to anyone. You still need mobile coverage, a satellite phone, a CB or HF radio or a beacon to reach help. The free Emergency+ app can also show your location, street address or what3words.

levels.name: Advice
levels.meaning: An incident has started. No immediate danger. Stay up to date.

levels.name: Watch and Act
levels.meaning: Conditions are changing. Start taking action now.

levels.name: Emergency Warning
levels.meaning: You may be in danger. Act immediately.

cards.title: Unresponsive person: DRSABCD and CPR
cards.when: Someone is not responding and not breathing normally.
steps: Danger: make sure the area is safe for you and the person. Do not put yourself or others at risk. Remove the danger or the person.
Response: loudly ask their name and squeeze their shoulders.
Send for help: if there is no response, call 000 and ask for an ambulance, or ask someone else to call. Do not leave the person.

Airway: check their mouth and nose are clear. If there is something there, roll them into the recovery position and remove any obvious blockage. Open the airway by gently tilting the head back and lifting the chin.

Breathing: look, listen and feel for up to 10 seconds. If they are breathing normally, put them in the recovery position, stay with them and keep checking. If they are not breathing normally, start CPR.

CPR (adult or child over 1 year): 30 chest compressions, then 2 breaths, and repeat. Push on the lower half of the breastbone, with your arms straight, about one third of the chest depth, at about 100 to 120 compressions a minute.
If you cannot give breaths, keep doing compressions without stopping. Compressions alone may still save a life.
Defibrillator: if an AED is available, attach it and follow its voice prompts. Do not leave the person alone or stop compressions to fetch one.
Keep going until they recover, a health professional takes over, or you are too exhausted to continue.
cards.call_000_if: Always, if the person is unresponsive. Babies under 1 year need a different technique: tell the operator and follow their instructions.

extra_sources.source_name: St John Australia - CPR (adult or child over 1 year)

cards.title: Snake bite
cards.when: Any known or suspected snake bite. Treat every bite as life-threatening, even if the person seems well.
steps: Get the person away from the snake. Do not try to catch or kill it.
Call 000 and ask for an ambulance.
Lie the person down, keep them still and calm.
If the bite is on an arm or leg, put a wide (10 to 15 cm) elastic roller bandage firmly over the bite as soon as possible.
Put a second roller bandage on, starting just above the fingers or toes and moving up the limb as far as you can reach. It should be tight: you should not be able to easily slide a finger under it.
Keep the limb still with a splint.
Write down the time of the bite and the time the bandage went on. If you can, mark the bite site on the bandage or skin with a pen, or take a photo.
If the person is unresponsive and not breathing normally, start CPR (see the DRSABCD card).
Stay with the person until the ambulance arrives.
do_not: Do not wash the bite area. Venom on the skin and clothes helps identify the snake.
Do not cut the wound or try to suck the venom out.
Do not try to catch or kill the snake.
cards.source_published: Wording follows the healthdirect page and the St John Australia fact sheet

extra_sources.source_name: St John Australia - Snake bite

cards.title: Heatstroke (very hot, confused or collapsed)
cards.when: Someone is very hot and has confusion, strange behaviour, seizures or has collapsed. Skin may be hot, red and dry, with little or no sweating.
steps: Call 000 and ask for an ambulance. Heatstroke is a life-threatening emergency.
Move the person to a cool or shady place. Loosen and remove extra clothing.
Start cooling them straight away. Best: put their whole body from the neck down in cold water for 15 minutes.
Or wet them with cold or cool water using a shower, hose, wet cloth or spray, and fan them continuously.
Put ice packs on the groin, armpits, cheeks, palms and soles of the feet.
Only give cool drinks if they are fully awake and can swallow.
If they stop breathing, start CPR (see the DRSABCD card).
do_not: Do not give paracetamol, aspirin or ibuprofen. They do not lower body temperature in heatstroke.

cards.title: Severe bleeding
cards.when: Bleeding that cannot be controlled with firm pressure, or signs of shock (pale, cold, clammy skin, fast weak pulse, faintness).
steps: Call 000 early. Follow DRSABCD.
Wear gloves if you have them. Lie the person down and expose the wound.
Press firmly, directly and continuously on the wound with your hands until bleeding stops. The person or a bystander can do this.
When you have a pad or dressing, put it on or in the wound and keep pressing.
If an object is stuck in the wound, press on either side of it and pad around it before bandaging.
Once bleeding is controlled, bandage the pad firmly in place. Watch for new bleeding.
If bleeding on an arm or leg is not controlled, apply an arterial tourniquet if you have one and tighten it until the bleeding stops. Warn the person it will hurt.
If bleeding is not on a limb and not controlled, use a haemostatic dressing if you have one, with firm pressure.
Keep checking their consciousness, breathing and pulse.
do_not: Do not give the person anything to eat or drink.
cards.call_000_if: Always, for severe or uncontrolled bleeding.

cards.title: Burns and scalds
cards.when: Burns from fire, hot water or steam, hot objects, chemicals or electricity.
steps: If clothing is on fire: stop the person moving, drop them to the ground, cover or wrap them in a blanket and roll them until the flames are out.

Remove the cause. Electrical burn: turn off the power if it is safe. Chemical burn: remove contaminated clothing and wash with water (you can keep going for up to 60 minutes). Dry chemicals: brush them off first.
As soon as possible, hold the burn under cool running water for at least 20 minutes. It can still help for up to 3 hours after the burn.
Take off clothing and jewellery from the area, unless it is stuck to the burn.
Cover the burn with a light, loose, non-stick dressing. Plastic cling film is a good choice, but do not use it on the face.
Watch for signs of shock.
do_not: Do not put lotion, cream, ointment or fat on a burn.
Do not remove anything stuck to the burn.
cards.call_000_if: The burn is deep (even if it does not hurt), is on the face, hands or genitals, has white, brown or black patches, was caused by chemicals or electricity, or affects the airway or breathing. Also get medical help for any burn bigger than a 20 cent coin.

extra_sources.source_name: St John Australia - Burn or scald

cards.title: Spider bite
cards.when: Bitten by a spider. Funnel-web and other big black spiders are dangerous. Redbacks are painful but not life-threatening.
steps: Funnel-web or any big black spider: call 000 and ask for an ambulance. Lie the person down and keep them still.

Funnel-web or big black spider: wrap a wide (10 to 15 cm) elastic roller bandage over the bite, then a second one over the whole limb from just above the fingers or toes upwards. Firm, but not cutting off circulation. Keep the limb still with a splint. Mark the bite site and write down the time.
Redback: wash the bite with soap and water and put a cold pack on it for 15 minutes. See a doctor if symptoms are bad, and go to an emergency department if the pain is very bad.
Other spiders: wash with soap and water and apply an ice pack wrapped in a cloth (never directly on skin). See a doctor if it gets worse.
Severe allergic reaction (difficult or noisy breathing, swollen tongue, tight throat, collapse): call 000. Use an adrenaline autoinjector if one is available.
do_not: Only use the pressure bandage for funnel-web or mouse spider bites, not for redback or other spiders.
cards.call_000_if: Funnel-web or other big black spider bite, difficulty breathing, collapse or confusion.

cards.title: Broken down or lost in a remote area
cards.when: Your vehicle is bogged or has broken down, or you are lost, far from help.
steps: Stay with your vehicle. It gives shade and shelter, and it is much easier for searchers to find than a person on foot, especially from the air.
Call for help if you can: 000 by satellite phone or mobile if you have coverage. If you carry a registered PLB or EPIRB, activate it.
Make your position easy to see from the air, for example by spelling a word in large letters on the ground.
Use the water and supplies you carry carefully. In hot, dry conditions, running short of water becomes life-threatening quickly.
Only leave the vehicle if you must. Leave a note that says the direction you are going, what supplies you have, and the date and time you left.
If you move, leave marks on the ground (such as rock piles or stick arrows) so trackers can follow you.
cards.call_000_if: Anyone is injured or in danger, or you cannot get back to safety.

cards.title: Flood and flooded roads
cards.when: Water over a road or creek crossing, flash flooding, or rising water around you.
steps: Never drive, walk, ride or play in floodwater. If it is flooded, forget it. Turn around and find another route, or wait.
Floodwater can be deeper and faster than it looks. It can take just 15 cm of flowing water to float a car.
Stay away from drains, culverts, creeks, causeways and low-lying areas.
If you are driving when flash flooding starts, avoid flooded roads and stop on the highest nearby ground, away from trees.

If you are trapped by rising water, get to the safest, highest place you can (this may be on the car roof or higher ground) and keep moving to stay above the water. Call 000. This is life-threatening.
For flood help that is not life-threatening, call the SES on 132 500.
cards.call_000_if: You or someone else is trapped by floodwater or in danger.

extra_sources.source_name: Victoria SES - Flood

cards.title: Bushfire while travelling (car)
cards.when: You see smoke or flames ahead, or a fire is threatening the road. Sheltering in a car is a last resort. It is extremely dangerous.
steps: If you see smoke or flames, turn around and drive away from the fire. Do not drive towards it. Do not try to outrun it.
Call 000 if your life is at risk. Say where you are. Check official warnings when you have signal.
Only if you cannot escape: park off the road in a clear spot, away from trees, scrub and long grass. If you can, park behind a wall or rock outcrop and face the front of the car towards the fire.
Turn on the hazard lights (most agencies also say headlights). Close all windows, doors and air vents. Stay in the car. Do not get out and run.
Get down below window level, for example in the footwell. Cover yourself with a woollen blanket. Drink water.
ENGINE AND AIR-CON: the agencies do not agree. Read your state's advice in the list below and follow it.
Stay down until the fire front has passed. Then get out carefully, because the car will be very hot. Move to ground that has already burnt, and check for spot fires.
do_not: Do not drive into smoke or towards a fire. Smoke can make it very dark and hard to see, and roads may be blocked.
Do not get out of the car while the fire front is passing.
cards.call_000_if: Your life is at risk, or once the fire front has passed if anyone is hurt.
cards.state_variants_title: What each state and territory says about the engine and air-con
cards.state_variants_intro: Engine OFF: NSW, VIC, SA, WA (VIC and SA say turn it off when the fire front is close). Engine LEFT RUNNING: QLD, NT. TAS: two Tasmanian sources differ. ACT: no in-car advice found. Advice can change. Follow the agency for where you are, any warnings, and the 000 operator.

state_variants.other: Also: headlights and hazard lights on, close windows and air vents, face the car towards the fire. Air-con is not mentioned separately.
state_variants.source_name: NSW RFS - Bush fire safety for travellers (PDF)

state_variants.engine: When the fire front is close: shut all vents, turn off the air-con and turn off the engine.
state_variants.other: CFA calls a stationary car in a clear area a last resort with a high risk of injury or death. Its Easy English guide says to turn the engine off when you park.

extra_sources.source_name: CFA - Stay safe in your car in a bushfire (Easy English PDF)

state_variants.engine: When the fire front is close: shut all vents, turn off the air-con and turn off the engine.
state_variants.other: Hazard lights on. Park off the roadway. CFS also says do not try to outrun a fire in a car.
state_variants.source_name: CFS SA - During a bushfire checklist

state_variants.other: Headlights and hazards on, close all vents and windows. Air-con is not mentioned. After the front passes, check for burning fires and do not move the car until it is safe.
state_variants.source_name: Queensland Government - Driving and bushfire awareness (source: Queensland Fire Department)

state_variants.agency: DFES (Department of Fire and Emergency Services)
state_variants.engine: Turn the air-con and the engine off.
state_variants.other: Call 000. Headlights and hazard lights on, close windows, doors and vents. DFES warns that sheltering in a vehicle gives only a slightly higher chance of survival than being caught in the open.
state_variants.source_name: DFES WA - Bushfire Travellers' Checklist, May 2019 (PDF, copy on a WA council site)

state_variants.engine: Run the air-con while you can. When the fire front is close, turn the engine off and close all vents.
state_variants.other: Hazard lights on. Park off the road. Be ready to get out as soon as the fire has passed. TFS's newer 2023 guide only lists a stationary car in a clear area as a last resort, with no steps.

state_variants.engine: Air-con off. The engine may be left running so the headlights keep working and the battery does not go flat.
state_variants.other: This differs from the TFS advice above. Headlights and hazards on, close all windows, doors and vents.
state_variants.source_name: Parks and Wildlife Service Tasmania - Bushfire safety

state_variants.agency: NT Government (Bushfires NT and NT Police, Fire and Emergency Services)
state_variants.other: Hazard lights on, close doors, windows and vents, lie on the floor and cover yourself with woollen or cotton fabric. Do not open the doors or windows until the fire front has passed. Air-con is not mentioned.

state_variants.engine: No advice about the engine or sheltering in a car found.
state_variants.other: ESA's bushfire pages and Bushfire Survival Plan do not give in-car steps. They say leave early, and if you are caught in a fire, protect yourself from the heat. Check esa.act.gov.au and the nearby NSW RFS advice above.

ambulance_cost_note.title: Ambulance costs
ambulance_cost_note.text: Calling 000 is free, but an ambulance is not always free. Medicare does not cover ambulance services, so you can be sent an invoice. Queensland and Tasmanian residents are generally covered by their state. Visitors to Queensland and Tasmania from other states are invoiced, and Tasmanians are not covered everywhere when interstate. South Australia says its ambulance service is not free or covered by Medicare. Check your ambulance cover or travel insurance before you travel. Costs and rules differ by state and change over time, so check the state ambulance service.
